title: Technical notes
text: How the numbers were produced. Code, parameters and result tables are in the project repository.

title: Technical notes
text:
Processing pipeline










Step
Input
Output
Method




1. LiDAR
2022 airborne LiDAR, streamed tile by tile
1 m ground (DEM) and surface (DSM) grids
ground returns → DEM; highest returns → DSM; each tile is downloaded, rasterised and deleted


2. Surface model
DEM, DSM, footprints, 2018 land cover, CHMv2
1 m building and tree heights
height above ground (nDSM) split into buildings (inside footprints), structures (bridges, viaducts) and trees (canopy mask)


3. Shadow casting
surface model, sun positions
sun / tree shade / building shade at every sample point and hour
a ray from each point (1.5 m above the ground) towards the sun, marched 1 m at a time for up to 1 km


4. Heat model (phase 10)
surface model, 2018 land cover, ERA5 hourly weather
mean radiant temperature and UTCI at 1 m, every hour; sampled at the same points
SOLWEIG 2022a on the GPU (solweig-gpu 2.0.0), in 1 km tiles with a 400 m margin, on a rented server


5. Edge attributes
DVRPC sidewalks and crossings, OSM bridges and covered walkways
metres of sun, tree shade and building shade per edge and hour; mean UTCI and metres per heat-stress class
sample points summed per edge; covered walkways always in building shade


6. Routing
edge table
shortest, shadiest and coolest path per walk
Dijkstra on length, on the shade cost of Wen et al. (2025) and on the heat (UTCI) cost, θ growing with distance walked


7. Walk samples
SEPTA timetable, residential parcels
one walk per home, stop → home
nearest frequent stop along the network, within 1.2 km


8. Summaries
walk metrics
tables by mode and walk length; stations; 500 m grid clusters
means within length bands; k-means on grid cells

title: Technical notes
text:
Key parameters









Parameter
Value




Dates and hours
June 24 and July 29, 2025, 8:00–19:00 local time, every hour (24 sun positions)


Sun time of an hour
30 min before the hour (15:00 = sun at 14:30), SOLWEIG’s convention for hourly mean radiation, for shade and heat alike


Grid resolution
1 m


Sample spacing along sidewalks
2 m


Observer height
1.5 m above the ground (above the deck on bridges)


Ray step and maximum length
1 m, 1,000 m


Minimum tree height
2 m


Shade cost (shadiest walk)
C = L_sun + (1 − 0.5θ) L_tree + (1 − θ) L_building + (1 − 1.5θ) L_indoor


θ curve (distance walked l, in m)
θ(l) = 0.3961 / (1 + exp(−0.0111 (l − 859.6))) + 0.1958


Frequent stop
≥ 6 departures per hour on one route and direction, weekday 15:00–19:00 (2026-10-28); all rapid-transit stations


Maximum walk
1,200 m along the network


Walk-length bands
under 300 m, 300–800 m, 800–1,200 m


No cooler option
the shadiest walk avoids less than 2% of the sun (sensitivity 1%, 5%, 10%)


Grid and clusters
500 m cells with at least 20 walks of 300–800 m; k-means, k = 3


Station ranking
at least 50 walks of 300–800 m


Heat model
SOLWEIG 2022a, GPU version solweig-gpu 2.0.0; global radiation split into direct and diffuse by the model; 153 sky patches for the sky view


Heat model tiles
1,000 m cores, each run with a 400 m margin on every side; 400 cores per day (those with sidewalk points)


Weather
ERA5 hourly via Open-Meteo, one cell (40.0° N, 75.25° W) for the whole city; rows 7–19 h


Tree heights in the heat model
canopy pixels above 40 m dropped (also in the shadow model)


Light through tree crowns
3% (fixed in SOLWEIG; tested at 5% and 15%)


Land cover for the heat model
2018 land cover → UMEP classes paved, building, grass, bare soil, water; canopy pixels take the class of the nearest non-canopy pixel


Heat cost (coolest walk)
C = Σ L (1 − θ r), r = (U_sun − U) / (U_sun − U_building), clipped to [−1, 1.5]; U_sun, U_building = hourly city medians of UTCI at sunlit and building-shaded sidewalk points


Extreme heat stress
UTCI ≥ 46 °C (heat-stress classes 26 / 32 / 38 / 46 °C, Bröde et al. 2012)

title: Technical notes
text:
Processing decisions

Streaming the LiDAR. The point cloud is far larger than the available disk, so each tile is downloaded, rasterised and deleted in turn. The horizontal coordinates are used as they are; the datum difference is about 1 m and matches the vector layers.
Roof holes. Dark or glassy roofs return no points, and filling them from the ground would make buildings disappear. Holes inside a footprint take the median height of the same building; buildings with less than 20% valid pixels use the recorded height.
Spikes and outliers. Isolated high returns (fewer than 2 neighbours within 10 m in a 5 × 5 window) are removed, and anything more than 400 m above the ground is treated as noise; one stray return near the TV masts otherwise cast kilometre-long shadows.
Holes outside buildings. Over water the surface takes the ground height; other holes are interpolated up to 10 px and otherwise take the ground, so river surfaces do not grow false structures.
Ground under bridges. Ground gaps are filled first from NOAA’s bare-earth model (bridges removed) and only then by interpolation, so bridge decks stay above the ground instead of being merged with it.
Leaf-off LiDAR. The survey was flown in March, so canopies have gaps. Inside the 2018 canopy mask, pixels below 2 m take the median of taller pixels in a 3 × 3 m window; a maximum filter was rejected because it raised the median tree height by about 5 m.
Trees outside the city. The land-cover layer stops at the city limit, so trees in the 1 km buffer come from CHMv2 (≥ 2 m); they only cast shadows onto city sidewalks.
Structures without footprints. Bridges and rail viaducts are kept as structures: areas at least 3 m high outside footprints and the canopy, cut where the surface jumps by more than 2 m, and kept if a piece covers at least 50 m² with a height spread of at most 3 m. Parked trains can pass this test too.
Flat-roof extrusion. Footprints with almost no LiDAR height (median below 2 m) but a recorded height of at least 3 m are built after the survey; they are extruded to the recorded height. Footprints where 30%–50% of pixels are tall overlap a neighbour and are skipped. In University City every extruded building was checked on 2025 aerial photos.
Bridge decks. A sidewalk segment is on a bridge when at least 80% of it lies within 15 m of an OSM road bridge and the two run within 20° of each other; its observer then stands on the deck. A plain intersection test would put every underpass on the bridge above it.
Covered walkways. OpenStreetMap covered walkways and passages are always building shade; in the heat model they take the hour’s median UTCI of building-shaded points (SOLWEIG does not see their roofs).
Cost function kept as published. The shadiest path sometimes has more sun than the shortest, when it trades tree shade for building shade (0.8% of test walks). The cost was kept unchanged, and the weighted exposure C is reported next to the sun share.
Which stops. Using every stop gave a median walk of 113 m, too short for any choice of route. Rapid transit plus frequent buses gives a median of 407 m and still reaches 82% of homes within 1.2 km.
Threshold for no cooler option. Sun reduction has a spike at exactly 0 (the shadiest walk is the shortest) and is continuous from about 2% on, so the cut is placed where the spike ends.
Clusters. Clustering uses only 300–800 m walks so that cells are compared at the same walk length. Silhouette scores for k = 3–6 are 0.35–0.37, so k = 3 is a summary of a continuum rather than natural types.
Campus footways. The regional sidewalk data lack most campus paths, so University City adds OpenStreetMap footways (36 km), leaving out sidewalks, crossings, private and indoor ways. Each mapped entrance is linked to the nearest sidewalk point without crossing a building; links over 30 m were checked by hand and the ones that are not walkable removed.
Two real days. The heat model needs real weather, so the calendar dates of the shade analysis (June 21, August 1) were replaced by the hot, sunny days nearest to them in 2025: June 24 (Philadelphia airport 101 °F) and July 29 (98 °F); August 1, 2025 was cool and overcast. The shadows were recomputed for the same days.
Own tiling. solweig-gpu can split a large area itself, but its tiles overlap only to the right and below, so a tower just left of or above a tile edge would cast no shadow into it. Every 1 km core is run on its own with a 400 m margin on all four sides and only the core is kept.
Tall ‘trees’. Façade returns beside towers and cranes appear in the canopy layer, up to 270 m tall. Canopy above 40 m is dropped in both models (2,573 pixels in the University City test domain, 0.1% of its canopy).
Points inside buildings. SOLWEIG has no UTCI on roofs. 32,933 sidewalk points that fall on a building pixel (footprints overlap the sidewalk lines) take the value of the nearest open pixel.
Bridge decks. SOLWEIG treats a bridge as a building and gives no UTCI on it. For the 30,346 points on bridge decks, UTCI is computed from the mean radiant temperature of the deck pixel.
One weather cell. Air temperature, humidity and wind are the same everywhere: ERA5 cells are about 25 km wide, and within-city differences in air temperature and wind are left for later work. The UTCI differences shown here come from radiation: sun, shade, sky view, walls and ground.
Pinned timetable. SEPTA replaced its GTFS feed during the project; the analysis uses the archived release v202609271, so stop frequencies stay reproducible.

title: Technical notes
text:
Validation

Synthetic shadows. Unit tests cast shadows from box buildings and trees on flat ground and check the shadow length against height / tan(sun elevation) for several sun positions, no shadow on the sunny side, tree versus building priority, terrain shadows and observers on bridge decks.
Building heights. LiDAR heights agree with the city’s recorded heights for 541,222 buildings (Spearman ρ = 0.84; Pearson r = 0.83). The median difference (LiDAR minus record) is −0.5 m, so LiDAR heights are typically 0.5 m lower than the records; the median absolute difference is 0.5 m.
Routing. With θ fixed, the search reproduces networkx Dijkstra exactly on 8,346 nodes (largest absolute difference 0). Hand-computed small networks check the cost rule, tree versus building shade and the indoor term.
Browser and analysis agree. The route tool’s JavaScript router returns the same shortest, shadiest and coolest paths as the Python analysis for 100 random walks, scenarios and hours, half of them with the heat cost.
Direction of travel. Reversing 500 walks of at least 400 m (home → stop) changes little: mean sun reduction 13.8% one way and 13.8% the other, correlation 0.99.
Visual checks. The University City entrances and passages were checked one by one on aerial photos.


The heat model

Two shadow models agree. SOLWEIG computes its own shadows. At the 3.6 million sidewalk points the two models agree on sun or shade at 90%–94% of points in every hour (Cohen’s κ 0.79–0.84). SOLWEIG finds slightly more shade (2.1% of points on average), as expected: it shades the ground, our rays start 1.5 m above it.
Complete coverage. Every sidewalk point has a UTCI value at every hour on both days, and no edge is without one.
Margin. The 8 cores with the most tall buildings 400–800 m away were rerun with an 800 m margin (155,764 points). UTCI changed by more than 0.1 °C at 0.16% of points at most and by more than 0.5 °C at 0.02%.
Light through tree crowns. 40 cores chosen across the range of canopy cover were rerun with 5% and 15% of the sun passing through crowns (SOLWEIG: 3%; measured values are about 1–5%, Konarska et al. 2014). Tree shade’s share of the building-shade relief at 15:00 is 112% at 3%, 110% at 5% and 99% at 15%.






Sensitivity of the heat model: light through tree crowns (left) and tile margin (right).

title: Methods
text:
Heights. 2022 LiDAR: ground, buildings and trees at 1 m.
Shadows. Every hour from 8:00 to 19:00 on June 24 and July 29, 2025, a ray from every 2 m of sidewalk towards the sun: building shade if a building, bridge or the ground blocks it, tree shade if only trees do, otherwise sun. The sun of an hour sits at half past the hour before (15:00 = 14:30), as in the heat model.
Heat. SOLWEIG turns the same heights and the weather into the UTCI, how hot it feels, at every square metre.
Sidewalks. Each sidewalk gets, per hour, its metres of sun, tree shade and building shade, and its UTCI.
Routes. Each walk has three routes: shortest, shadiest (shade cost) and coolest (heat cost).

Every hour from 8:00 to 19:00 on June 24 and July 29, 2025, a ray from every 2 m of sidewalk towards the sun: building shade if a building, bridge or the ground blocks it, tree shade if only trees do, otherwise sun. The sun of an hour sits at half past the hour before (15:00 = 14:30), as in the heat model.

title: Methods
section: The cost of a sunny metre
text:
The cost of a sunny metre
The shadiest walk uses the cost function of Wen et al. (2025):
\[C = L_{\text{sun}} + (1 - 0.5\,\theta)\,L_{\text{tree}} + (1 - \theta)\,L_{\text{building}} + (1 - 1.5\,\theta)\,L_{\text{indoor}}\]
A sunny metre costs 1, tree shade 1 − 0.5θ, building shade 1 − θ, an indoor metre 1 − 1.5θ. θ grows with the distance already walked, so shade matters more the longer the walk:





θ as a function of distance already walked.




With θ near 0.2 for the first 500 m, a short walk only leaves the shortest route when that costs almost nothing.

title: Methods
section: The cost of a hot metre
text:
The cost of a hot metre
The coolest walk keeps θ but values each metre by its UTCI:
\[C_{\text{heat}} = \sum_{\text{edges}} L\,(1 - \theta\,r), \qquad r = \frac{U_{\text{sun}} - U}{U_{\text{sun}} - U_{\text{building}}}\]
\(U\) is the sidewalk’s UTCI; \(U_{\text{sun}}\) and \(U_{\text{building}}\) are the city medians in sun and in building shade at that hour (15:00: about 45.3 and 40.5 °C). A typically sunny metre costs 1 and a typically building-shaded one 1 − θ, as in the shade cost; everything in between follows its UTCI (\(r\) kept between −1 and 1.5). Indoor passages have no UTCI, so the coolest walk stays outdoors.

title: Methods
text:
Walks home from transit
Every home within 1.2 km of a frequent stop is one walk, stop to home (431,114 walks). Results are reported by length (under 300 m, 300–800 m, 800–1,200 m), since short walks rarely have an alternative, and for rapid transit and buses separately.
The direction does not matter: walking home to stop instead gives a mean sun reduction of 13.8% against 13.8% (500 walks, correlation 0.99).

title: Methods
text:
Metrics







Metric
Definition




Sun



Sun share
metres in the sun on the shortest walk ÷ its length


Sun reduction
(sun on shortest − sun on shadiest) ÷ sun on shortest


Weighted exposure reduction
(C of shortest − C of shadiest) ÷ C of shortest


No cooler option
the shadiest walk avoids less than 2% of the sun


Heat



UTCI of a walk
length-weighted mean UTCI along it, in °C


UTCI reduction
UTCI of the shortest − UTCI of the coolest (or shadiest) walk, in °C


Extreme heat stress
metres with UTCI ≥ 46 °C


Both



Detour
(length of the walk − shortest length) ÷ shortest length


Indoor Contribution Index
(1 − Lshadiest ÷ Lshortest, outdoor) × indoor share of the shadiest path’s shade (Wen et al. 2025)



Weighted exposure falls about a tenth as much as sun: with θ near 0.2, each metre of sun avoided lowers C by only 0.15–0.2 m.

title: Methods
text:
Indoor scenarios (University City)
Mapped entrances are linked to the nearest sidewalk; passages through buildings count as indoor walking. Three cases: outdoor only, plus buildings open without a Penn ID, plus all mapped buildings. The shortest route is always the outdoor one.

title: Methods
text:
How we checked
The five stations with the largest sun reduction were checked on aerial photos; checks of the heat model are in the technical notes.

title: Data
text:
The heat model
Shade says where the sun is blocked, not how hot a sidewalk feels. For that, the same heights go into SOLWEIG, which computes the radiation a standing person receives from sun, sky, walls and ground and, with the weather, the UTCI: how hot it feels, in °C. Above 38 °C is very strong heat stress, above 46 °C extreme.
The model needs real weather, so the study uses two hot, sunny days of 2025: June 24, during a heat wave, and July 29. Shadows are computed for the same moments.

One ERA5 cell covers the whole city, so air temperature and wind are the same everywhere; the heat map varies with sun, shade, walls and ground. The model ran in 400 one-kilometre tiles per day on a GPU and gives a UTCI value at all 3.6 million sidewalk points, every hour.

title: Data
text:
Whose walks
Each walk starts at a rapid-transit station (Regional Rail, L, B, T tunnel) or at a bus stop with at least 6 buses an hour (15:00–19:00), and ends at a home within 1.2 km on foot: 431,114 walks. The other 91,659 homes (17.5%), mostly in the Northeast and Roxborough, have no frequent stop that close.





Homes without a frequent stop within 1.2 km (red).

title: Data
text:
University City
In University City, entrances and indoor passages of 41 buildings were mapped (4.4 km; 10 buildings open without a Penn ID), and campus footpaths from OpenStreetMap were added.

title: Data
text:
Known gaps

Campus and park paths are missing outside University City, so cooler options there are understated.
Two clear, hot days; trees from leaf-off LiDAR and 2018 land cover, buildings from 2022.
One weather cell for the city: no neighbourhood differences in air temperature or wind. Trees let a fixed 3% of the sun through.
Missing footprints, new buildings and temporary objects affect shade locally.
The timetable is one weekday in fall 2026.

title: Results
text:
From sun to heat
The UTCI is how hot the weather feels, in °C. On June 24 at 15:00 a typical sunlit sidewalk felt like 45.9 °C, at the edge of extreme heat stress (46 °C); a step into shade took off about 5 °C.

tree shade against sun








Median UTCI of sidewalk points in the sun, in tree shade and in building shade, by hour (shade classes from our shadow model). Bands: UTCI heat-stress categories.





Tree shade is as cool as building shade. The shade cost counts it as half as good; in the heat model it takes off 112%–115% of the step from sun to building shade at 15:00 (94% at 8:00). Shaded streets still receive heat from walls and pavement that stood in the sun; a tree also shades the ground under it.
Shade does not make a walk comfortable. Building shade stays at very strong heat stress from 10:00 to 17:00 on June 24.

UTCI = mean along the walk, change against the shortest. Extreme heat = metres with UTCI ≥ 46 °C, and the reduction for walks that have any.

The two walks mostly agree: for 71%–77% of walks of 300–800 m they are the same. Where they differ, the coolest walk takes the tree-lined street.
A little cooler for a little more distance: about 0.1 °C cooler than the shadiest walk and 1.4–2.2 times the cut in extreme heat, for detours of 0.3%–0.9%.
Rapid-transit walks gain most: −0.72 °C against −0.54 °C from bus stops.
Averages hide the walks with no choice. The gain is largest in the morning (−0.82 °C at 09:00), small around midday (−0.33 °C at 14:00) and again in the evening (−0.13 °C at 19:00), when the low sun no longer heats the sunny side much.



Why the coolest walk is cooler





Same detour, cooler walk: mean detour and mean UTCI reduction of walks of at least 300 m at 15:00 (both days), for three costs with θ fixed from 0.05 to 0.6.




At the same detour the UTCI cost cools walks 12%–14% more than the shade cost. Counting tree shade as building shade adds only about 1%: most of the gain comes from differences within each shade class, such as sun next to hot walls against sun on a lawn.
Robustness. With 5% or 15% of the sun passing through tree crowns instead of 3%, tree shade’s share of the building-shade relief at 15:00 moves from 112% to 110% and 99%, still far from the half assumed by the shade cost. See the technical notes.

Opening the mapped buildings puts about one in five shadiest walks indoors and removes another 1.9–2.3 points of sun, without longer walks. The Indoor Contribution Index stays near zero: passages here are an equally long, cooler option, not a shortcut, unlike the malls and linked towers of Wen et al.’s Dubai stations. Indoor routes are taken mainly when they are on the way; walks of 800–1,200 m use them 2.4–3.0 times as often as walks of 300–800 m.

title: Results
text:
Limitations

Campus and park paths are missing outside University City, so cooler options there are understated.
“No cooler option” mixes two cases: no cooler street, or one not worth the detour.
Two hot, sunny days in 2025; trees from leaf-off LiDAR and 2018 land cover; buildings from 2022.
One weather cell: no neighbourhood differences in air temperature or wind.
Trees let a fixed 3% of the sun through.
Indoor passages assume open, air-conditioned buildings; they have no UTCI.
